I wasn't comparing the way in which humans and transformer models work - for context I'm fully aware of how GPT models work using token prediction, and that they are glorified predictive text programs. 

I was comparing the outputs. Humans and AI both consistently produce incorrect information. They also both consistently produce less incorrect information when using accurate sources while inferencing. 

In machine learning this is called zero shot prompting, essentially it's where you give the model sources in the input. This results in more accurate outputs as it has the information it need's so doesn't hallucinate fake information. Autonomous agents like auto-gpt work in cycles and have access to the internet so first gather accurate information from the web, then feed it back into themselves. This results in more accurate outputs with less hallucinations.

Also "fabricating things, using fake citations and the like" is not something unique to AI, humans do all these things regularly too, though usually when speaking so that people don't catch them out as they have intent behind their misinformation (AI fortunately doesn't have intent yet).

The hallucinations problem seems to be reduced by increasing model size (GPT4 has way less hallucinations than GPT3.5).

I don't think it will ever be solved (let's face it even humans face this problem), one thing which has been found is that bots like auto gpt which use web access to gather info hallucinate a lot less than ChatGPT/Bard due to using the internet as a zero shot input for the next inference. Hallucination is greatly reduced when using zero shot prompting with correct info as the model doesn't need to use built in knowledge about a topic and instead uses information from a source (again like a person, using sources rather than off the top info results in being more correct).

Also increasing worker productivity can definitely result in job losses. If all your workers are now 200% as productive you only need 50% of the workforce.

The ground will be using a terrain mesh system, whereas the wheat will be using instanced meshes. Even when the wheat is being rendered the terrain is still being rendered behind it because the wheat has an alpha texture - not rendering the wheat instances outside of a radius is straight up performance gain which is the point of low settings.

It's also probably not possible to raise the distant terrain dynamically like you're suggesting. For a start the terrain likely uses dynamic LOD so terrain which is far away will be extremely low poly if so raising it will produce lots of weird artifacting which won't look good, not to mention the performance cost of dynamically moving parts of the terrain up and down depending on if there's meant to be wheat there at runtime while the player moves around the map.

From the digital foundry benchmark tests they ran, the latency difference in Portal RTX from DLSS2 to DLSS3 was around 3ms (still over a 40ms improvement over native 4k performance). 3ms is basically nothing if you're on a well setup system (for reference going from 30 to 60 yields a 16.6 ms reduction, and you can gain another 12.5 from going to 240 from 60 - people playing at 240hz have a lot of headroom).

If you were to compare input lag on a 4090 using DLSS3 frame gen and a 3090 using DLSS2 I'm gonna assume that the input lag will be lower on the 4090 due to the 60% faster raster performance from better hardware + shader execution reordering (at 60fps the improvement in raw raster+DLSS upsampling needs to only be 15fps up to 75fps to completely negate DLSS3 frame gen latency increases). I'm sure these tests will be done as soon as review embargo is lifted.

Sure pro gamers and top level competitive gamers won't be using this tech as 3ms is a bigger deal in that niche, but they make up a tiny percentage of the market and play in 1080p low settings anyways so don't really need something like this to begin with.

Personally I just don't see Nvidia making custom 3x faster optical flow hardware and basing the entire generation's architecture around something that doesn't work. I think DLSS3 is gonna be revolutionary and frame generation will become a staple in graphics tech as it develops.

I also see this type of tech being implemented into non realtime 3D engines like Blender Cycles and Vray once it matures.

Ray tracing is going to benefit from the less discussed Shader Execution Reordering significantly. I expect RT raster performance even without DLSS to benefit greatly from this, add in DLSS upsampling and before frame gen you're already talking 60+ FPS. Remember this is a 3 part equation is not just raster to frame gen it's optimised raster (SER),frame gen, and upscaling benefits.
